1. Executive Summary
This report summarizes the Risk Management processes applied to the Illinois Basin – Decatur Project (IBDP) and the
subsequent results. The primary objectives for the Risk Management processes applied to the IBDP were to:
    1) Identify and treat important risks to project success; and
     2) Develop iterative risk management procedures in a general carbon capture and storage (CCS) context.

The IBDP is one of seven Regional Carbon Sequestration Partnerships initiated by the US Department of Energy to carry out
regional characterization and field projects to demonstrate the capability to permanently and safely store carbon dioxide (CO2)
and provide the information basis for commercial-scale projects. This endeavor was carried out in three phases:
       Phase I: Characterization,
       Phase II: Validation, and
       Phase III: Development.

This report focuses on the Phase III Risk Assesment and Management efforts of the IBDP.

To date, the IBDP has conducted three workshops at which risks were identified and evaluated. The first and second workshop
sessions were conducted in Stage 1 (at project start-up) and the third was conducted in Stage 2, after a substantial tonnage of
CO2 had been injected. All three workshops involved a broad spectrum of project staff and outside experts, and resulted in a
prioritized (ranked) list of risks based on the numerically aggregated, expert-weighted opinion of all participants.

To develop detailed risk management plans and the potential treatments to be applied, the Stage 1 risk workshops were
organized in breakout groups by discipline; this allowed a smaller number of participants to focus on developing specific risk
response actions (risk treatments) for potential implementation. Technological advancements enabled the Stage 2 workshop
to be conducted entirely in plenary session.

The risk-bearing scenarios and treatments identified in the Stage 1 workshops centered primarily on topics related to project
design and construction and geologic uncertainties. These areas had been largely addressed by the beginning of the Stage 2
workshop, where the primary issues included the potential for felt seismicity and the challenges of maintaining consistent plume
tracking, largely due to challenges resulting from new applications of technologies. Risk Management topic areas for all three
workshops also focused on plans and treatments for risks associated with health and safety, budget, and public interactions.

In Stage 1, substantial effort was applied to establish a tracking system for the execution of risk treatments and the resultant
effects of the treatments on risk levels. After an initial staff-intensive period of implementation, the system was streamlined to
focus on two goals:
   1) Providing adequate information to support anticipated project decision points; and
   2) Maintaining a culture of risk awareness throughout the project’s lifecycle.

Although Stage 1 data capture on risk treatment and tracking status proved to be challenging, the process led to important lessons
learned, and the collected information was adequate to support the decision to initiate CO2 injection in November 2011.

Additionally, outside the purview of this report, perhaps the most powerful risk management tool was the culture of risk awareness
that was cultivated and facilitated in the field and during planning operations during which numerous safety meetings were held
that included operations specific job safety analyses based upon the scenarios and events described within this report.

4. Risk Management for the IBDP
4.1 Scope and Terminology
The scope of risk management for the IBDP corresponds directly with the scope of the IBDP itself. The aims of the project —
expressed in the SOPO and the Project Values (page 11) — describe the entities against which risk is identified, analyzed,
evaluated, and treated. Given this extensive scope, the broad purpose of risk management is to clear paths toward the project’s
goals by identifying and removing potential challenges (wherever possible), and to proactively continue doing so as the project
progresses, and changes occur in its status, knowledge base, and environment.

Project risks are managed through the chained processes of risk assessment, risk evaluation, treatment definition, treatment
tracking, and re-assessment, and evaluation. For the IBDP, risk assessment focused initially on broad entities called Features,
Events, and Processes (FEPs), and later on more specific entities called scenarios. For the risk assessment performed at project
start-up, fundamental risk concepts were defined (including project values and risk scales), and project information was reviewed
to create a common basis for evaluation. Risk assessment results (based on FEPs) were applied to drive the creation of a set of
scenarios, which in turn were applied to create a set of risk treatments. Tracking the completion status of the risk treatments
continues to provide the basis for re-evaluating risk at critical project junctures and decision points such as the start of injection.
These processes are detailed in Section 4.6, Risk Treatment and Risk Tracking (page 23).

Terminology related to risk management processes are not identical in all contexts, and continues to evolve even within the
context of GS. The terminology used in this report (see Table 2) generally follows the definitions in International Standards
Organization Risk Management Standard ISO 31000 and those in Canadian Standards Association CCS Standard z741-2012.

Risk Definition
Within industrial risk assessment, risk is typically defined as the product of the severity and likelihood (or probability) of an event
that may impact one or more project values. This definition, already in use by Schlumberger, was adopted for the IBDP.

Severity and likelihood are typically semi-quantified through expert judgment on multi-step categorical scales, although in narrow
contexts some components (such as financial impacts) can be quantitatively estimated. In some systems, additional attributes
such as observability and treatability are factors in risk quantification.

Workshops included areas of technical consideration – geologic distribution and engineering, and areas of non-technical
consideration – public engagement, legal and regulatory, infrastructure. In both cases project staff and outside experts participated
in the assessment of associated risks with the category in which they were most familiar.

Risk Scales
Quantification using Relative Scales
In risk evaluation, quantification most often means that descriptions of risk and risk components are expressed in ranking or
ordinal numbers (i.e., first, second, third, etc.) rather than measurable cardinal numbers (1.725, 1897.2, etc.). This property is
acceptable and useful for several reasons:

1) Ordinal numbers empower project managers to order (prioritize) concerns and actions;
2) Ordinal numbers allow simultaneously ranking priority across disparate scales, such as one scale involving environmental
impact and another involving project schedule; and
3) Ordinal scales can be rapidly applied through expert judgment, without waiting for rigorous estimates of measured quantities.

Risk values can become rigorously quantitative if either: a) Large numbers of observations establish the recurrence frequency of a
well-defined chain of events, or b) A well-defined scenario involving a well-defined system can be numerically modeled using well-
validated software. Given that neither a) nor b) is the case for most risk matters that concern IBDP, all risk quantities addressed
herein are expressed in ordinal numbers.

As noted above, risk is quantified here as the product of its components severity and likelihood (SxL). Both severity (S) and
likelihood (L) are quantified on five-category scales. As these scales involve a mix of judgmental and potentially observable or
measurable criteria, they are overall categorical/ordinal. When risk evaluation was designed for IBDP, it was apparent that
conceptions of typical or ordinary levels of severity and likelihood had to be distinguished from conceptions of worst case.
Accordingly, quantities of upper-bound, best-guess, and lower-bound were defined for both S and L. Collecting six data points for
each risk element proved to not only require great effort, but also add complexity to the data analysis. As detailed later in this
report, collecting only three of these quantities proved to be a better practice, yielding similar quantifiable results. The three
surviving risk component quantities are Sub (severity upper-bound), Sbg (severity best-guess), and Lbg (likelihood best-guess),
where Lbg is the likelihood that impacts having severity = Sbg will occur. No discrete likelihood value is (nor can be) associated with
Sub.

Severity
Against each project value, a range of potential negative impacts is expressed according to a categorical five-point severity scale
(Appendix 7.1). The impact scale is categorical (as opposed to being a function of measured values) because many impacts (and
the aggregate of multiple impacts) can be judged and expressed more consistently in relational words than in numbers. There are
five categories because that scheme allows adequate impact differentiation while also allowing rapid and consistent judgment by
subject-matter experts. Though other numbers of categories are used, five-point severity scales are common within industrial risk
management. The purpose of the severity scale is to provide a consistent basis by which to compare impacts within a project
value.

For the project values that are in typical industrial usage, the impact ranges and categorization are also typical. For the Research
and Industry Viability values, category definitions were developed specifically for the IBDP. Depending on the specific scenario, an
undesired event could have impacts to more than one project value: For example, the potential failure of CO2 storage could entail
environmental and/or health and safety impacts. For the IBDP, a financial impact of CO2 lost from storage was also assumed,
resulting from a hypothetical financial penalty under a carbon-price assumption of USD $30 per ton. Where impacts may affect
multiple project values, the most severe potential impact defines the severity value.

For each project value, the category descriptions are only examples of relative impact magnitudes; they do not embrace the full
variety of conceivable impacts. Categorizing potential impacts across multiple values is necessary for comparing risks and for
rationalizing treatments. However, impacts of the same level in two different project values are viewed as equal only in the sense
that they motivate similar levels of attention and effort in risk treatment.

Likelihood
The likelihood of negative impact is also categorized in five levels. Because actual experience with GS projects is not yet sufficient
to estimate recurrence intervals for many pertinent events, experts were asked to estimate Likelihood based on their expectations
relative to an arbitrary standard of 100 similar projects during 100 years (Appendix 7.1). The planned project duration is ten years
including three years of post-injection monitoring, but analyzing a longer time period is necessary so that potential longer-term
effects are not ignored. The Likelihood scale presents a roughly categorized version of probability that provides a consistent basis
for comparison.

In other projects and contexts, it is common to use arithmetic or roughly logarithmic scales of probability values, such as <1%,
<3%, <10%, <30%, <90%, in place of the comparison (with a number of other hypothetical projects) that was used for the IBDP.
Each type of scaling is arbitrary, and neither one is measurable, so the choice of scale type rests largely upon what system is
most easily conceived and applied by the risk evaluators. During workshops and through spreadsheets, risk evaluators appeared
to have applied the categorized Likelihood values with facility and consistency.

Risked Entities: FEPs and Scenarios
Various types of entities exist for which the probability and severity of negative impact (i.e., the risk) might be evaluated. At one
end of the spectrum, the impact ranges and occurrence probabilities of narrowly defined events might be found in historical
(actuarial) data gathered about occurrences identical to those that could occur at the project. Without actuarial data, experts can
still make near-quantitative judgments about the probability and severity of relatively well-defined chains of events (scenarios). At
the other end of the spectrum, risk levels can be holistically — yet more qualitatively — associated with broader concepts
important to the project. For results to be applicable toward defining risk treatments, any project risk evaluation must define
specific scenarios, but to provide the latitude for envisioning the critical aspect of unfamiliar risks, any project risk evaluation
should also consider broad concepts. These may be considered as an initial step towards scenario evaluation or as check for
thoroughness afterward. Risk identification for a new project should not be limited to evaluating a pre-defined list of scenarios.

Both scenarios and broad concepts were evaluated for the IBDP. To avoid missing sources of risk by focusing too narrowly, risk
assessment at Stage 1 began with FEPs. FEPs evaluated by the large workshop group as having higher risk were used as the
basis for writing scenarios. Risk levels for individual scenarios were monitored informally by individuals assigned as Responsible
or Accountable for each scenario (see page 23). The Stage 2 evaluation was conducted using the cumulative project experience
and a more specific list of scenarios for tighter focus risk evaluation. The following sections describe this progression in greater
detail.

Stage 1 FEP List
The list of FEPs evaluated by each working group was selected from the FEP database created by Quintessa Ltd. for CO2
sequestration projects (see www.quintessa.org), with some modifications and additions specific to the project. The Quintessa list
captures most of the sources of risk that should be considered for a generic CCS project, but specific characteristics of any
individual project are likely to extend the list. The IBDP FEPs list includes many FEPs typical of large-infrastructure projects such
as vehicle hazards and chemical exposures, and also includes distinctive CCS-related FEPs in these areas:
       Reservoir porosity, permeability, and other geologic uncertainties;
       Induced seismicity;
       Groundwater contamination;
       Data access and archiving;
       Integration of surface- and subsurface-engineered components;
       Internal and external project communications;
       Regulatory developments; and
       Post-injection monitoring requirements.

Stage 2 Scenario List
The Stage 2 risk assessment exercise was designed to identify and evaluate the risk elements (FEPs or scenarios) considered
important to further project progress, rather than to specifically re-evaluate all the risks from Stage 1. To begin the process, a set
of scenarios (rather than FEPs) was selected. Operational experience at mid-project promoted a more detailed focus on project
related risks reducing the potential to miss important general areas of risk. The Stage 2 scenario set was seeded from the Stage 1
scenarios that remained active as risk sources (37 of 94 scenarios), then supplemented by 96 additional scenarios gathered
during a pre-workshop process focusing on the changes in the project environment and knowledge (Table 4). This combined list of
133 was refined to a total of 83, with two scenarios added during the workshop, for a total of 85 scenarios discussed and
evaluated for Stage 2.

Timing and Design
Initial risk evaluation was conducted through two face-to-face workshops (Stage 1, Parts 1 and 2) held at the offices of the Illinois
State Geological Survey (ISGS) in Champaign, Illinois. Each of the two Stage 1 workshops incorporated mainly internal experts,
plus a small number of external experts and representatives of the public.

The first of the two Stage 1 workshops was conducted February 19-21, 2008, in conjunction with the general project kickoff
meeting. The kickoff meeting was attended by project participants from all member organizations, and a broad range of expertise
was available for both evaluation workshops in Stage 1. The second of the two Stage 1 workshops was held July 15-16, 2008.
Most of the participants involved in the two Stage 1 risk workshops visited the project site and contributed to a half-day’s sharing
of information on project data, plans, and risk-assessment methods.

During the project’s early months, about 25 individuals met for two-to-three days to carry out the initial risk workshops, and
approximately 15 additional person-days were spent by a smaller risk assessment team. The Schlumberger Carbon Services Risk

Site information and plans were presented by the participants most familiar and involved with the project and its physical and
cultural setting. Presenters compared well-known site features with those less well-known, and identified uncertainties with
potentially important consequences.

Training in risk-assessment techniques and procedures included a discussion of heuristics (rules of thumb that individuals apply,
often unconsciously, when they make decisions under uncertainty). Although paying attention to heuristics and biases, judgment
under uncertainty, and risk perception is important to workshop design, the pursuit of precise and repeatable expert-elicitation data
through rigorous techniques is constrained by practical resource limits and human patience. The Stage 2 Workshop later in the
project made improvements in this regard (see Changes in Technique, page 19).

The effectiveness of discussion and the efficiency of data acquisition for the risk assessment were improved in Stage 2 over the

A risk treatment (internally called a risk response action during Stage 1) is intended to lower risk associated with a well-defined
scenario by reducing either the likelihood that the scenario will occur, the severity of consequences if it does occur, or both. As an
example, for a scenario involving injury caused by mechanical failure of energized or rotating equipment, one risk treatment would
be to improve the equipment quality to reduce the likelihood of failure; another would be to ensure that personnel wear adequate
protective gear. Contingency plans and other preparations for unexpected or uncommon events constitute risk treatment through
severity reduction.

In theory, the effectiveness and resource efficiency of each treatment in reducing its target risk(s) can be catalogued and up-to-
date risk status and treatment progress can be aggregated from bottom-up data whenever desired. In practice, this high degree of
monitoring demands considerable internal resources. Consequently the approach now taken is periodic summary reporting at a
relatively generalized level (see Risk Reporting following), augmented by more rigorous and quantitative stage-gate-oriented
review.

RACI Definition of Responsibilities in Risk Management
A common way for project managers to assign responsibility for project activities is within a RACI matrix. In this respect, risk
treatment activities are no different, and the RACI tool has been applied. This standard project management acronym indicates
persons or entities (individuals or groups) that are Responsible, Accountable, to be Consulted with, or to be Informed about an
action. In Stage 2, IBDP uses the modified acronym ROCI, where O indicates Oversight. The Responsible assignment is for
those who do the work to accomplish the task. Accountable (Oversight) is assigned to those who are answerable for ensuring that
the task is completed correctly and thoroughly; the individual or group accountable also delegates the task to those who will be
responsible to do the work. Consulted parties are those whose views and input are wanted, typically subject matter experts.
Informed are those persons or entities that are kept up-to-date on the progress.

5. Risk Management Lessons Learned
5.1 Risk Assessment Processes
The main process changes and Lessons Learned in the progression from Stage 1 to Stage 2 were:

     1.  Discussion and evaluation were held with all evaluation participants present (in plenary session), rather than in breakout
        groups by discipline. As risks can easily be missed in the gaps and overlaps between project components, between
         project functions, among partner organizations, and among professional disciplines, this format proved to be superior.

          Lesson Learned: Discussion and evaluation in whole-group (plenary) session was preferable to breakout sessions,
           as it led to fully involving all experts, airing a wider range of views, and promoting greater discussion among
             professional disciplines.

     2.  The qualifying expertise for evaluating risks within topic areas was determined not through breakout-group assignment,
         but by self-rated expertise level. During data analysis, each severity or likelihood value chosen was correlated with the
         expertise level of the person who provided it. This enabled the identification of instances in which expert views may
         diverge from those of well-informed non-experts.

          Lesson Learned: Self-rating of expertise level led to a more efficient means to understand how expert views
            diverged from those of well-informed non-experts.

     3.  Using a wireless keypad system made changes #1 and #2 (above) practical. The system recorded all severity and
          likelihood values and instantly displayed results on screen, flagged potential needs for further discussion, was more
        engaging for participants, much faster, and was error-free in archiving data.

          Lesson Learned: A wireless keypad system for instantaneous feedback and display was beneficial and had the
           added advantage of archiving data easily.

     4.  Three risk quantities, not six, were collected per risk element. Data were collected strictly in the order Sub > Sbg > Lbg (see
        Risk Scales, page 29, for explanations of these quantities). The three-value quantification was clearer for participants and
         simpler to analyze, and it more clearly distinguished the upper-bound or worst-case severities.

          Lessons Learned:
                  1) Three risk quantities per element are adequate and easier for participants to analyze;
                  2) Scenarios with very high worst-case severities must be treated differently from scenarios whose high risk
                   results from higher likelihood.

     5.  Spreadsheet follow-up was used to complete the workshop evaluation; it became clear that the desire to distinguish
        group vs. individual evaluations was an unnecessary complication.

          Lesson Learned: There is no need to distinguish group vs. individual in evaluations.

5.2 Risk Information Management
     1.   In addition to process changes for risk assessment, project experience has shown the need for improved information
       management and internal reporting. Although not yet fully achieved, the key goal for risk information management is a
         simple, easy-to-manage strategy.

          Lessons Learned:

              1) Maintaining staff focus on actions helps to reduce and control major risks;
              2) Monitoring lesser and changing risks provides the basis for elevating them if necessary; and
              3) Incrementally accumulating the data to support risk-based project decision-making at key turning points is
              beneficial to project success.

     2.  Risk information is dominated by many-to-many relationships: Every scenario inevitably involves multiple FEPs; one FEP
       can generate multiple scenarios; one scenario may have several risk treatments; and one treatment may reduce risk from
         multiple scenarios. Topical groupings are also non-unique: A scenario that seems clearly to fall within one topic group may
       have its most important treatment within a different topic group, as would be the case for a scenario involving a monitoring
          activity that could incite public opposition to the project.

          Lesson Learned: While flat spreadsheets are ideal for handling one-to-one and one-to-many relationships, the
           many-to-many relationships typical of risk information are often better handled using a relational database. It should
           be noted that inputs and outputs from such databases are still two-dimensional spreadsheets.

     3.  Changes made in risk information management since project commencement have reduced the amount of administrative
        time required. Because current tools have not satisfactorily supported the real-time collection and application of risk
         information, developing a process for ongoing, yet minimally burdensome participation, is the key to engaging project staff.

         Lesson Learned:  It is recommended that future multi-partner CCS projects consider a) Adopting a risk information
          management system already in use by one partner (if a suitable system exists); or b) Licensing such a system from
           a commercial vendor.

5.3 Ongoing Risk Management
Along with the area of risk information management, ongoing risk management shares the challenge of producing usable and
critical results while adding as little as possible to project overhead. While command-and-control approaches are suitable for some
easily defined high-exposure activities, they can add greatly to staff burdens if applied to all risks, and can increase some risks if
the approach demands constant attention. The appropriate level and style of attention is not easily understood nor reached.

Compared to a concrete project management topic like well construction, or to a topic demanding constant attention like budget,
risk can be challenging to grasp and to focus on. Efforts to collect, evaluate, manage, and deliver risk information build the
framework for successful risk management, but in the first instance, these elements must serve to motivate project staff to
constantly envision project risks and risk remedies.

While the spreadsheets, checklists, and other tools of the trade are useful, the most important product of a successful risk

6. Conclusion

A Risk Management process was applied to the IBDP that helped to identify and treat risks. The process was iterative and
adaptive as more was learned about CCS. Three risk workshops were conducted in the IBDP, two of which were prior to injection
and one during the injection phase. The risk workshops and risk management techniques helped the project to operate safely and
achieve its objectives.

To date, the IBDP safely stored one million tonnes CO2 and is, at the time of this report, in the post-injection monitoring phase.
The lessons learned from IBDP have been and continue to be applied to subsequent CCS projects. Much of the success of the
IBDP can be attributed to the culture of safety and risk awareness that was cultivated and facilitated in all aspects of the project by
the personnel involved.
